title: Mass changes when a reactant or product is a gas

notes.definition: Some reactions appear to break the law of conservation of mass because the measured mass goes up or down. This happens in non-enclosed (open) systems when a reactant or product is a gas whose mass has not been measured.
explanation: Mass is always conserved in a chemical reaction because no atoms are lost or made. However, when you measure the mass of a reaction mixture in an open container, the reading on the balance can change. This is because gases can move into or out of an open container. The balance only measures what is inside the container, not the gas in the surrounding air.

If a reactant is a gas, the mass of the solid or liquid product can be greater than the mass of the starting material. For example, when magnesium is heated in air it reacts with oxygen: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). The magnesium oxide has a greater mass than the magnesium because it contains oxygen atoms that came from the air. The mass of oxygen was not measured at the start, so it looks as if mass has been gained.

If a product is a gas, the mass of the reaction mixture can decrease. For example, when a metal carbonate is heated it undergoes thermal decomposition: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). The carbon dioxide escapes into the air, so the solid left behind has a smaller mass than the solid at the start. The same happens when a carbonate reacts with an acid in an open flask, or when a metal reacts with an acid to give hydrogen gas.

The particle model explains these changes. In a gas the particles are far apart and move quickly and randomly in all directions, so gas particles can spread out of an open container and escape. Gas particles from the air, such as oxygen molecules, can also move in and react. In a solid or liquid the particles stay close together, so they stay in the container and are weighed.

If the same reaction is carried out in a closed system, such as a sealed flask or a syringe, no gas can escape or enter, so the total mass stays the same. You can use the change in mass of an open system to calculate the mass of gas given off or taken in: mass of gas = difference between the starting and final masses. This is useful in practical work, such as following the rate of a reaction by measuring the loss in mass as carbon dioxide escapes.
keyFacts: Mass is always conserved; apparent changes are due to gases entering or leaving an open (non-enclosed) system.
If a reactant is a gas (for example oxygen from the air), the mass of the product can increase.
Metals heated in air gain mass because they combine with oxygen to form metal oxides.
If a product is a gas (for example carbon dioxide or hydrogen), the measured mass can decrease as the gas escapes.
Thermal decomposition of metal carbonates gives off carbon dioxide, so the mass of solid decreases.
In a closed system the total mass stays the same.
Gas particles are far apart and move randomly, so they can escape from or enter an open container.
Mass of gas given off = starting mass − final mass.

keyTerms.definition: An open system where substances, especially gases, can enter or leave, for example an open flask or crucible.
A system where no substances can enter or leave, for example a sealed flask.
The breaking down of a substance into simpler substances using heat.
In this context, the gain of oxygen by a substance, for example a metal reacting with oxygen to form a metal oxide.
A model in which all matter is made of tiny particles; gas particles are far apart and move randomly, so gases spread out.
A compound containing a metal and the carbonate group, CO₃, such as calcium carbonate, CaCO₃.

equations.name: Mass of gas lost or gained
equations.formula: mass of gas = final mass − starting mass (positive if gas was gained, negative if gas was lost)

workedExamples.title: Mass gained when a metal is heated
workedExamples.question: A student heats 2.4 g of magnesium ribbon in a crucible. After the reaction the magnesium oxide has a mass of 4.0 g. Calculate the mass of oxygen that reacted and explain why the mass increased.
steps: Mass of oxygen = mass of magnesium oxide − mass of magnesium.
The mass increased because oxygen atoms from the air combined with the magnesium. The oxygen was not weighed at the start.
workedExamples.answer: 1.6 g of oxygen; the product contains oxygen atoms from the air.

workedExamples.title: Mass lost in thermal decomposition
workedExamples.question: A crucible containing calcium carbonate has a mass of 35.20 g. After strong heating to constant mass it has a mass of 32.56 g. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide given off.
steps: The decrease in mass is the carbon dioxide that escaped: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂.

workedExamples.title: Percentage change in mass
workedExamples.question: 12.35 g of copper carbonate is heated until it has completely decomposed into copper oxide. 7.95 g of copper oxide remains. Calculate the percentage decrease in mass.
steps: Decrease in mass = 12.35 − 7.95 = 4.40 g (this is the mass of CO₂ lost).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that when mass decreases in an open flask, atoms have been destroyed.
misconceptions.right: In fact the atoms are still there, but some are in a gas that has escaped into the air, so they are no longer weighed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a metal gets heavier when heated because heat adds mass.
misconceptions.right: In fact heat has no mass. The metal combines with oxygen atoms from the air, and these atoms add to the mass of the product.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think gases have no mass, so losing a gas does not change the mass.
misconceptions.right: In fact gases are made of particles that have mass. When carbon dioxide escapes, the mass on the balance falls by the mass of the gas.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the law of conservation of mass does not apply to reactions involving gases.
misconceptions.right: In fact it applies to every reaction. If all the gas is collected or the system is sealed, the total mass stays the same.

realWorld: Bakers rely on carbon dioxide gas escaping from dough: a loaf loses mass while baking partly because carbon dioxide and water vapour escape.
Lime (calcium oxide) is made in lime kilns by heating limestone; the mass of solid falls by almost half as carbon dioxide is driven off.
Rusting iron gains mass as it reacts with oxygen and water from the air, which is why a rusty iron object can weigh more than the original iron.
examTips: Always say where the gas comes from or goes to: 'oxygen from the air is added' or 'carbon dioxide gas escapes into the air'.
Use the particle model in explanations: gas particles move randomly and spread out, so they leave an open container.
If a question asks why the mass seems to change, say that mass is still conserved but the gas has not been weighed.
In calculations, the mass of gas lost or gained is just the difference between the two balance readings.
When heating magnesium in a crucible, the lid is lifted occasionally to let oxygen in, but not too much, so magnesium oxide smoke does not escape.
summary: Mass is always conserved, but open systems can appear to gain or lose mass.
A gaseous reactant (such as oxygen) added to a solid makes the measured mass increase.
A gaseous product (such as CO₂ or H₂) escaping makes the measured mass decrease.
Gas particles are far apart and move randomly, so they can escape or enter.
In a closed system the mass does not change.
Mass of gas = difference between start and end masses.

A student heats magnesium ribbon in an open crucible.
What happens to the mass of the solid in the crucible?

It decreases
It stays the same
It decreases then returns to the start value

Hydrogen

Carbon monoxide

It decreases because carbon dioxide escapes
It stays the same because mass is conserved
It increases because the acid is used up
markScheme: 1 mark: it decreases because carbon dioxide escapes
questions.explanation: The flask is open, so the carbon dioxide made leaves the flask and is no longer weighed. Mass is conserved overall, but not in what the balance can measure.

questions.question: Which of these is a closed system?
options: An open beaker
A crucible with its lid lifted
An evaporating basin
A sealed flask with a bung
markScheme: 1 mark: a sealed flask with a bung
questions.explanation: Only a sealed container stops substances getting in or out. The others are open to the air.

questions.question: Which reaction would show an increase in mass if it was carried out in an open container?
options: Zinc reacting with sulfuric acid
Copper carbonate being heated
Iron wool being heated in air
Sodium carbonate reacting with hydrochloric acid
markScheme: 1 mark: iron wool being heated in air
questions.explanation: Iron reacts with oxygen from the air (a gaseous reactant), so the solid gains mass. The other three all produce a gas (hydrogen or carbon dioxide) that escapes.

questions.question: Which statement explains why gases can escape from an open flask?
options: Gas particles have no mass
Gas particles are far apart and move randomly in all directions
Gas particles are attracted to the air
Gas particles are smaller than solid particles
markScheme: 1 mark: gas particles are far apart and move randomly in all directions
questions.explanation: In the particle model, gas particles move quickly and randomly and spread out, so they leave the open container. Gas particles do have mass, and their size is not the reason.

questions.question:
Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid in a sealed flask:
Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
What happens to the total mass of the flask and contents?
options: It decreases because hydrogen is made
It increases because zinc chloride is made
It stays the same
It decreases because the zinc dissolves
markScheme: 1 mark: it stays the same
questions.explanation: The flask is sealed, so the hydrogen cannot escape. No atoms are lost or made, so the total mass is unchanged.

questions.explanation: 6.2 − 4.0 = 2.2 g. The decrease is the mass of carbon dioxide gas that escaped; no mass was destroyed.

Table 1 shows the results. All the magnesium reacted.
Calculate the mass of oxygen that reacted.

questions.question:
A student heats copper carbonate until it has completely decomposed into copper oxide.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage decrease in mass.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: decrease = 12.35 − 7.95 = 4.40 g
questions.explanation: The mass lost is the carbon dioxide (4.40 g). Divide by the starting mass, not the final mass: 4.40 ÷ 12.35 × 100 = 35.6%.

questions.question:
A student heats magnesium in a crucible until it has all reacted.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage increase in mass.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 0.80 − 0.48 = 0.32 g
questions.explanation: The gain is the oxygen added (0.32 g). Percentage increase = 0.32 ÷ 0.48 × 100 = 66.7%.

questions.question: Explain why the mass of magnesium increases when it is heated in air.
markScheme: 1 mark: magnesium reacts with oxygen (from the air) to form magnesium oxide
1 mark: the mass of the oxygen that combines is added to the product (oxygen was not weighed at the start)
questions.explanation: The product contains both magnesium and oxygen atoms. The oxygen came from the air, so it was not counted at the start.

questions.question: Explain why the mass of the solid decreases when calcium carbonate is heated in an open crucible.
markScheme: 1 mark: calcium carbonate decomposes to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide
1 mark: carbon dioxide is a gas and escapes into the air
questions.explanation: The carbon dioxide leaves the crucible, so only the calcium oxide is weighed at the end.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.
markScheme: 1 mark: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)
questions.explanation: Calcium carbonate breaks down into solid calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas. The (g) shows why mass is lost from an open container.

questions.question:
A student adds marble chips to acid in an open flask.
The student says:
'The mass went down during the reaction, so mass was not conserved.'
Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide gas was produced and escaped from the open flask
1 mark: no atoms were lost or made; the gas still has mass but was not weighed
questions.explanation: If the reaction were done in a sealed flask, the mass would stay the same. The apparent loss is only the escaped gas.

questions.question:
A student adds marble chips to acid in an open flask on a balance. The mass decreases.
Suggest how the student could change the experiment to show that mass is conserved.
acceptedAnswers: collect the gas in a balloon
markScheme: 1 mark: carry out the reaction in a closed system (sealed flask or balloon over the flask)
1 mark: so the carbon dioxide cannot escape and is weighed with the flask
questions.explanation: If the gas stays inside the system, the balance reading does not change. A balloon over the neck of the flask is safer than a tight bung, which could be pushed out by gas pressure.

questions.question:
A student does two reactions in open flasks.
Reaction 1: zinc and dilute sulfuric acid.
Reaction 2: copper sulfate solution and sodium hydroxide solution.
The mass of the flask in reaction 1 decreases. The mass of the flask in reaction 2 does not change.
Use the particle model to explain the difference.
acceptedAnswers: gas particles move randomly and spread out
markScheme: 1 mark: zinc and acid produce hydrogen gas
1 mark: gas particles are far apart and move randomly, so they spread out of the flask
1 mark: copper sulfate and sodium hydroxide produce a solid precipitate and a solution, with no gas, so all products stay in the flask
questions.explanation: Only gases can escape from an open flask. Solid and dissolved products stay where they are and are still weighed.

questions.question:
A student heats copper in air, weighs it, then heats it again.
Table 1 shows the results.
Explain why the mass did not change after the second heating.
acceptedAnswers: no more copper to react with oxygen
markScheme: 1 mark: all the copper has reacted with oxygen
1 mark: so no more oxygen can be added and the mass stays constant
questions.explanation: Heating to constant mass shows the reaction is complete. The increase of 0.80 g is the oxygen that combined.

questions.question: Name the gas that combines with a metal when the metal is heated in air.
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen
questions.explanation: Air is about 21% oxygen, and hot metals react with it to form metal oxides, increasing the mass of the solid.

questions.question:
A student carries out two experiments.
Table 1 shows the results.
Explain both results. Include balanced equations in your answer.

headers: Substance heated in an open crucible

markScheme: Indicative content: Experiment 1: 2Ca + O₂ → 2CaO; oxygen is a reactant from the air; its mass was not measured at the start; product contains the extra oxygen atoms so the mass increases. Experiment 2: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; carbon dioxide is a gaseous product; it escapes from the open crucible; so the mass of solid decreases. In both, mass is conserved overall; no atoms lost or made.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both results clearly explained in terms of gas entering or leaving, with correct balanced equations.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one result explained, or both described with little explanation or without equations.
questions.explanation: The key idea is that open containers let gases in and out. A gas reactant adds mass that was not weighed; a gas product removes mass that is then not weighed.

questions.question: Describe how you could carry out an experiment to find the mass of oxygen that reacts with a sample of magnesium ribbon. Explain how you would make sure your result is accurate.
markScheme: Indicative content: weigh an empty crucible and lid; add coiled magnesium ribbon (cleaned with sandpaper) and reweigh; mass of magnesium by subtraction; heat strongly with a Bunsen burner on a pipe-clay triangle on a tripod; lift the lid occasionally with tongs to let air in; replace the lid quickly so magnesium oxide smoke does not escape; continue until the magnesium no longer glows; cool and reweigh the crucible, lid and contents; reheat and reweigh until the mass is constant (all magnesium has reacted); mass of oxygen = final mass − mass of crucible, lid and magnesium; safety: do not look directly at burning magnesium, wear eye protection, hot crucible.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear, logically ordered method including weighing before and after, letting in oxygen while preventing loss of product, heating to constant mass, and the calculation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with weighing before and after and some steps for accuracy.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as heat magnesium and weigh it, with little detail.
questions.explanation: The important points for accuracy are heating to constant mass so all the magnesium reacts, and controlling the lid so oxygen gets in but magnesium oxide does not escape.
